questions.problem:
Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/2|}}{4},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following vectors:

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $-3{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=0.$

II. ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ only if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

III. The set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent.
questions.worked_solution:
We say that three vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are *linearly independent* if the only solution to the equation

$$
{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3}=0
$$

is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

With that in mind, let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3} & =-3[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12+0+2 \\ 3+6+4 \\ 0+0+10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 13 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. The equation ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=0$ corresponds to the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we can reorder the equations in this system as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system using back substitution, we find that the solution is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0.$

- Statement III is true. Since statement II is true, the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Remember that we can factor a constant out of the norm, provided that we take the absolute value of the constant:

$$
‖kw‖=|k|\cdot ‖w‖
$$

Using this fact and the formula for the norm, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-\frac{w}{5}‖ & =|-\frac{1}{5}|\cdot ‖w‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{{w}_{1}^{2}+{w}_{2}^{2}+{w}_{3}^{2}+{w}_{4}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{4+16+4+1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\sqrt{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 5 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $u=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],v=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]$ and $w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ be vectors such that $u\,⊥\,w.$ Find $(w+v)\cdot (2u+3w).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $u$ and $w$ are orthogonal vectors, we have that $u\cdot w=0.$ Therefore, using linearity of the dot product to expand the parentheses, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(w+v)\cdot (2u+3w) & =2(w\cdot u)+2(v\cdot u)+3(w\cdot w)+3(v\cdot w) \\  & =0+2(v\cdot u)+3(w\cdot w)+3(v\cdot w) \\  & =2(v\cdot u)+3(w\cdot w)+3(v\cdot w) \\  & =2(-4\cdot 5+(-2)\cdot 1+2\cdot (-3)+(-4)\cdot 3) \\  & +3(1\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-5)+2\cdot 2+2\cdot 2) \\  & +3(-4\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot (-5)+2\cdot 2+(-4)\cdot 2) \\  & =2(-40)+3(34)+3(2) \\  & =-80+102+6 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function 

$$
f(x)=3{x}^{2},\,0\le x\le 1.
$$

Calculate $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{2}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{2}]={\int }_{S}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We compute the expected value of ${X}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,{x}^{5}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
